opus-5.5.text:
I think language is an incredibly powerful tool, but we sometimes forget what it actually is. Language is a communication protocol that humans invented to pass information between each other efficiently. It's highly compressed and highly abstract, and that's exactly why it works so well for communication. But that same property makes it a limited substrate for an intelligent system to model the world.

When I say "a cup falls off the table," you immediately understand it. That's because you already have a rich internal model of physics, space, gravity, and what a cup is made of, built through years of seeing, touching, and interacting with the world. The sentence is just a pointer into that model. It doesn't contain the model. So if a system learns only from language, it's learning from pointers, from the shadow of the real thing. It can become very good at manipulating those symbols, and large language models have shown how far that can go. But a lot of what makes intelligence grounded isn't captured in text, because humans never needed to write it down. Nobody writes a paragraph explaining how light reflects off a curved surface before picking up a glass. That knowledge is tacit.

There's also a bandwidth issue. The amount of information in visual and sensory experience is enormous compared to text. A child, by age four, has taken in more raw visual data than the largest text corpora we train on. Much of it is redundant, but that redundancy is part of how you learn invariances, causality, object permanence, and so on. Language skips all of that and hands you the conclusions.

So my view is that language is something like the last mile of intelligence, not the foundation. It's a great interface, a great way to reason abstractly and to align systems with humans. But if we want systems that truly understand the physical world, that can plan, act, and imagine consequences, I think we need to build representations from perception and interaction first, something closer to a world model, and then let language sit on top of that, rather than expecting language alone to carry everything.

r001.rationale: The response says language is useful for abstract reasoning and as an interface; it does not deny that language is a tool for thinking.

r002.rationale: It describes language as compressed and abstract for efficient communication, and says those same properties limit the information it carries for modeling the world.

r003.rationale: The cup-falling example says the sentence conveys an outcome while relying on an internal model of physics, space, and gravity that the sentence itself does not contain.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest starting point is that language is a lossy compression of the world. It's an incredibly efficient one, because humans spent a very long time shaping it so that we can transmit ideas to each other with very few bits. But the thing it compresses is a world that we already perceive and understand through our bodies, through vision, through interaction. Language sits on top of that. It doesn't replace it.

So when people say a large language model has learned a world model from text, I think they're half right. There's an enormous amount of structure about the world that gets reflected in text, and these models recover a surprising amount of it. But there's also a huge part of the world that nobody ever bothers to write down, precisely because it's so obvious to anyone with eyes. Nobody writes "when I let go of the cup it falls toward the table, and the liquid keeps moving for a moment after the cup stops." Nobody writes how light wraps around an object, or what happens when you look at a scene from a slightly different angle. That knowledge is in the pixels, not in the sentences. If your only sensor is text, you inherit the blind spots of what people chose to say.

The second limitation is that language is discrete and symbolic, and the physical world is continuous and geometric. You can describe a room in words, but the description is always underdetermined. There are infinitely many rooms consistent with any paragraph. An intelligent system that has to act in that room, navigate it, manipulate things in it, needs a representation that is much richer than the paragraph. I'd argue that's where a lot of the real difficulty in intelligence lives, in that gap between the symbol and the thing.

The third thing, and this is maybe more philosophical, is that language is a tool for communication, not necessarily for thinking. A lot of what my brain does when I catch a ball or recognize a friend from behind has nothing to do with words. The "reasoning" happens in some representation that was never linguistic. We've made the convenient assumption that because our reasoning traces come out as text, the underlying computation should be text. I'm not sure that's true. It might be an artifact of what we could measure.

That said, I don't want to overcorrect. Language is also where abstraction lives. It's how you get concepts like "fairness" or "next Tuesday" that don't have a pixel-level signature. So the way I think about it is not language versus vision, it's that language should be the interface, and the thing underneath should be a model grounded in perception and in the structure of the physical world. The representation does the heavy lifting; language is how you query it and how you explain it to another agent.

Where that becomes concrete for us as researchers is in asking what the visual representation itself should look like, and whether it can be learned to a level of quality where it is doing real modeling work rather than just producing captions for a language model to consume. Right now a lot of multimodal systems treat the vision side as a translator into tokens. I think that undersells what vision is for. The world is the ground truth, and language is one view of it.

r001.rationale: The response says language is “not necessarily” a tool for thinking and that some brain processes are nonlinguistic. It does not clearly deny that language can be a tool for thinking.

r002.rationale: It describes language as lossy compression shaped to transmit ideas with few bits, linking communication’s efficiency to information that gets left out.

r003.rationale: It gives examples of physical events that people do not write about, but does not clearly contrast language’s ability to represent event outcomes with its omission of the underlying dynamics.

astra-6.text:
I think language is an incredibly powerful tool, but it’s also a compressed representation of the world. When we describe something, we select what matters to us and leave out a huge amount of information. That’s useful for communication, but we shouldn’t assume that everything we leave out is irrelevant to intelligence.

For example, imagine trying to describe how a piece of cloth moves when you pick it up. You can say, “It folds,” or “It drapes over my hand,” but those words don’t capture all the geometry, the motion, or the physical interactions. And you can have an intuitive understanding of those things without being able to articulate it. A child can learn to interact with objects long before they can explain what they’re doing.

So I would distinguish between language as an interface and language as the underlying representation. Language might be a very good interface for asking a system questions or giving it instructions. But that doesn’t mean the system should represent everything internally through language. It may need representations learned directly from images, video, and interaction with the world.

The limitation is really in treating what we can say about the world as equivalent to the world itself. Language captures a lot of our knowledge, but an intelligent system should also be able to learn from what we haven’t put into words.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes language as an interface from internal representation, but does not deny that language is a tool for thinking.

r002.rationale: It says language selects what matters and leaves out information, explaining that this compression is useful for communication while omitted information may still matter to intelligence.

r003.rationale: The cloth example contrasts words such as “folds” or “drapes” with the geometry, motion, and physical interactions they omit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language is a very powerful abstraction, but it is also a bottleneck. When we describe something in words, we select a small part of what is actually there—the part that matters for communication. We leave out a huge amount of information about geometry, motion, physical relationships, and the details of our experience.

For example, you can say, “There is a cup on the table.” That tells you something semantic, but it doesn’t tell you precisely what the cup looks like, how it is balanced, or what will happen if you push it. You can add more words, of course, but a description is still a selective representation of the situation.

So I would distinguish learning from what people say about the world from learning from the world itself. Language gives us access to a tremendous amount of accumulated human knowledge. But I don’t think we should assume that everything an intelligent system needs to understand must pass through language. Vision, and potentially interaction, can provide information and structure that people never bother to put into words.

The interesting question is how to bring those sources together without forcing all of them into a purely linguistic representation.

r001.rationale: The response calls language powerful but limited and says it is not the only source of understanding; it does not deny that language is a tool for thinking.

r002.rationale: It says words select only a small part of what is present—what matters for communication—and leave out information an intelligent system may need, such as geometry, motion, and physical relationships.

r003.rationale: It says language does not tell us what will happen if the cup is pushed, but does not contrast a representation of event outcomes with omitted underlying physical dynamics.
